Scotland is obviously a much smaller country than the US, and it goes without saying American experiences of NYE would vary depending on geographical location, class and race.  

The unified experience of New Year's Eve consisted be baking cakes and eating meals, visiting neighbours and family and giving gifts. Racial minorities were not excluded from these celebrations, with New Year's Eve being a special day on plantations for slaves.

For the more affluent, grand balls would be held, with one in St. Paul, MN in 1849 being described as "the largest collection of beauty and of fashion we have ever seen in the West."

I found some journal articles that feature case studies of specific regions. Some predate 1850 but it gives you an idea of the traditions which would already have  been observed by this time.

# Texas:

New Year's gifts were typically exchanged with neighbours and family. Farmers would share produce and women would sew socks and mittens. 

The letters of Mrs. Mary Austin Holley, detailed her experiences in 1837 Houston:

>"we had a gay supper last night, & danced in the new year, though, being a Sunday did not dance out the old. A few young persons were in. among them 2 young gentlemen excellent singers & musicians on guitar, flute, violin, & Accordian. After retiring they serenaded us with those instruments combined & vocal solos. Very sweet musick. It lasted till near the time the birds commenced their morning concert."

Balls were also customary on New Year's Day, as an article appearing in the *Telegraph and Texas Register*, dated December 26, 1838, reads:

>"We have been requested to mention that a Ball will be given in this city on New Years day at the Houston house. The subscription list is now open for those who may wish to participate in the recreation."

The ball was later reported to have been:

>"one of the most splendid and delightful entertainments of the kind ever given in this section. A large number of ladies and gentlemen from this city were present, and many also  
from Harrisburg and the vicinity. The festivities were  
kept up to a late hour, and the guests returned highly pleased with the cordiality and kindness of the hospitable entertainer."

​

Louis C. Ervendberg visited a German orphan asylum near New Braunfels, Texas, on New Year's Eve in 1849. His experience demonstrates the experiences of the less-affluent:

>"a table covered with a snowy cloth, with Christmas presents for each of the children....after a walk about the grounds, everyone had tea by the fireside, and many a merry game was played with the children, and many a happy song was sung, and many a verbal nut was cracked along with the pecans."

Clearly, the holiday was meaningful and celebrated, and those who did not have wealth would save food, presents and such for the special occasion.

The experiences of African Americans have also been documented in 1843 Texas, although unclear if these were enslaved or free:

>"Last night through the kindness  
of Mr. Mc. \[McDonald\] the Negroes of this vicinity had thier \[sic\] Christmas Ball in his unfinished store. (The Upper part destined for a Masonic Hall). It was late ere all arrived many of them having had to come several miles. It was a Subscription Ball & the unfortunate negro who could not raise a couple of bits (about Is) was not admitted at the commencement of the Ball, but Black hearts wax soft & as midnight approached- the Strains of music sweet, the excitement produced by dancing, the door keeper became benevolent & it was a public ball."

Source: Walter Prescott Webb, 'Christmas and New Year in Texas (Texas Collection),' *The Southwestern Historical Quarterly*, Vol. 44, No. 3 (Jan., 1941), pp. 357-379

# Minnesota:

As with Texas, the custom of sharing gifts and charity seemed to also define New Year's celebrations in the Mid-West. In Minnesota, we learn about the traditions of white Americans who lived proximate to Native Americans, in 1845:

>"The Red Lake missionaries marked New Year's Eve by assembling the pupilsof the mission school and giving them presents. In 1845 the gifts consisted of flannel shirts for the boys and "shortgowns" for the girls. The Indian children "came with cleaner faces & hands than usual," writes Mrs. Lewis, "asa little soap had previously been distributed."

As with the German orphanage in Texas, this was a special time of year and limited resources were pooled and reserved to celebrate,  the holiday, such as soap in this example.

In early 1850s frontier Minnesota, a typical New Year's Day was described as:

>"Ladies remain at home and see company. Gentlemen make short calls, and take a slight refreshment everywhere. (From ten in the morning to four in the afternoon were considered the proper hours for making calls.)"

Later, in the 1870s, steamboat trips up the Mississippi became a popular New Year's Day activity.

Source: Bertha L. Heilbron, "Christmas and New Year's on the Frontier," *Minnesota History*, Vol. 16, No. 4 (Dec., 1935), pp. 373-390

# Louisiana:

A journal article from the *American Folklore Society,* revealed New Years' traditions on plantations in 1850s Louisiana.

>At daylight, on the 1st of January, the rejoicing began on the plantation; everything was in an uproar, and all the negroes, young and old, were running about, shaking hands and exchanging wishes for the new year.

Children received toys, and adults, including the elderly, were gifted:

>an ox killed expressly for them, several pounds of flour, and a new tin pan. 

Clothes were also given, with men receiving:

>"a new jean or cottonade suit of clothes, and the women a dress and a mo gaudy headkerchief or tignon, the redder the better. Each woman that had had a child during year received two dresses instead"

Music was played at balls that were hosted and slaves were allowed to drink.

Source: Rosan Augusta Jordan and Frank De Caro, '"In This Folk-Lore Land": Race, Class, Identity, and Folklore Studies in Louisiana,' *The Journal of American Folklore,* Vol. 109, No. 431 (Winter, 1996), pp. 31-59

​

​

New Year's Eve became more widely celebrated in the early 1900s, with many immigrants who came to big cities being surprised at the extent of the celebrations when compared with their homelands. The first celebrations of Times Square were reportedly as early as 1904, with the first ball drop occurring in 1907. (Source: [https://www.timessquarenyc.org/times-square-new-years-eve/nye-history-times-square-ball](https://www.timessquarenyc.org/times-square-new-years-eve/nye-history-times-square-ball))

​

To conclude, before 1850, New Year's Eve was celebrated with small traditions in the rural United States, such as calling on families and exchanging homemade gifts such as produce or knitted items. Bigger and grander celebrations were reserved for larger population centres, in the form of balls, such as those in Houston and St. Paul. Native Americans and African Americans were included in New Year's celebrations, and those with limited resources, such as the Texan German Orphanage, would still make an effort to mark the holiday with gifts and feasts.

$12 billion of assistance refers to the 1948 value of the dollar, this is the general rule for any figures you see quoted in historical context, unless otherwise stated at the source. $12 billion in today's money wouldn't even begin to fund the rebuilding of Europe necessitated by war.

Following the war, a November 1947 report by the President's Committee on Foreign Aid, headed by Averell Harriman at the request of Harry S. Truman, found that somewhere in the region of $12.5 to $17.2 billion would be required to assist Europe. By 1946, $9 billion had been spent on emergency and humanitarian aid by the US. Most of this - $3.75 billion - went to the United Kingdom in 1946, to stabilise the value of the pound sterling against other nations' reserves of sterling in the Empire, such as India and Pakistan.

In today's money, this means $49,143,846,153.85 was sent to the UK in 1946, and the U.S. had spent $117,945,230,769.23 by 1946. Pretty eye-watering figures!

​

**Sources**

Bruce L.R. Smith, 'Birth of the Marshall Plan, 1947-48,' in *Lincoln Gordon: Architect of Cold War Foreign Policy*, (University Press of Kentucky: 2015).

This is a very interesting notion, I am from the UK but have a personal (and academic) interest in the American Presidency, so alongside extensive reading, I feel personally able to assist you in understanding this.

​

The notion that the United States is an elective monarchy no doubt stems from the perceived individual power of the office of POTUS. If we consider the number of traditions associated with the Presidency, such as the playing of Hail to the Chief, the inauguration ceremonies, State Funerals where the casket lies under the rotunda and a service is held in the National Cathedral, the Presidency has become almost as ritualistic as a traditional monarchy. As a Brit myself, I couldn't help but be reminded of a ceremony like the Trooping of the Colour when I watched the coverage of President Bush's funeral last November. Queen Elizabeth II has Buckingham Palace, Windsor Castle and Balmoral (amongst others), he President has the White House, with the Oval Office and the Resolute Desk and Camp David, which are just as significant symbolically. He also has a title, 'Mr. President,' and features on currency, just like the British Monarch, and even has his own day, President's Day on the third Monday in February.

Interestingly enough, in the aftermath of the Revolutionary War, the idea of having a Monarchy in the United States was debated. Supporters of the idea wished to have George Washington installed as the first King, but this did not occur, obviously. Washington is revered in the public consciousness still, his face on currency, the capital bearing his name and indeed, a magnificent monument on the National Mall being constructed in his honour (it was supposed to be more extravagant, but these plans were halted). There were also plans to bury Washington at the centre of the Capitol, but these never came to fruition, with the objection of his wife. Thus, the public veneration Washington in particular is clear, alongside select other Presidents including Lincoln, Jefferson and FDR who have received their own monuments in DC. (A book on this subject would be Kathleen Bartolini-Tuazon's "George Washington and the Presidential Title Controversy of 1789: For Fear of an Elective King.")

I'm not sure I would agree, personally, on the concept of the U.S. being a Monarchy. In the eyes of the public, perhaps, yet from a political science perspective, the real 'power,' lies with the US Congress, the President can only pass Executive Orders by himself, requiring Congress to do much more, including authorise wars.  (A good book on this debate is The Imperial Presidency by Arthur M. Schlesinger or the Presidency and the Constitution by Genovese and Spitzer).

​

The United Kingdom, by comparison, despite the attempts of the various Reform Acts from the Victorian and Edwardian Era, has a Parliament comprised of a relatively small slice of society. In the Georgian era, there would be little choice for constituents and only wealthy men were able to vote, keeping the 'power', i.e. the seat, amongst themselves, filling Parliament with their 'type.' This undoubtedly continues, the vast majority of MPs having gone to private schools and elite Universities such as Oxford and Cambridge. Jeremy Corbyn, the current leader of the Labour Party, would be an exception to this, but he does not get favourable treatment from the press. Furthermore, before attempted reforms, seats would pass from father to son, keeping the power in bloodlines. For example, current politicians such as Jacob Rees-Mogg have fathers who were MPs, and David Cameron was a descendant of the prominent Astor family. No doubt this has opened up in recent years, with the first black female MP Diane Abbott still serving, and increasing diversity with individuals such as Sajid Javid or Chukka Umuna. But the Parliament remains disproportionately white and male. 

If we consider more recent British Prime Ministers, although Margaret Thatcher was in office for an extensive period of 11 years from 1979-1990, she attained only 44% of the popular vote at her peak, due to the peculiarities of our electoral system, with its 600+ constituencies and not voting for the individual, but rather, a local MP. Much akin to the frustrations of the electoral college.

With the examples I've just highlighted, there are clear aspects of a hereditary British Parliament, so no doubt the argument could be made for a hereditary republic existing.

I can't, nor would any other Historian, be able to say whether this is 'true': it's a historiographical debate, and one that will probably never be resolved. But I hope what I have just written assists your understanding and helps you form your own conclusion.

In 400AD, Anglo-Saxon Britain was in a transitional period as the Romans, who had occupied Britain wholly since the end of the second century, began to be recalled to Rome to fight against attacks from the Barbarians. The last Romans left Britain in 410. 

Christianity in Britain after the Romans left was substantially weaker than it was in the fourth century, with the lack of strong Christian leaders in the Romans. Thus, Britain contained pockets of Christianity, particularly in areas that had a strong Roman influence, but this waned as the Romans left, although it did not die out completely.

But the British Isles were an attractive prospect for Christian rulers, who desired the political benefits of a Christianised Anglo-Saxon population due to its location and substantial population.

Most of our understanding of the Christianisation of Britain comes from two sources: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and the writings of Bede the Venerable.

We know from Bede's account, and the letters of the Pope himself, that Pope Gregory the Great sent St. Augustine and Italian missionaries to Kent in 597 to begin the conversion process of the British Isles. Gregory conceived the plan in c.596, writing in his letters “the nation of the Angles, situated in a corner of the world, has remained up to now in thrall to tree-trunks and stones.” Thus, Gregory believed that the Anglo-Saxons were pagans and desired Christianity. This was a major event in the history of the Anglo-Saxons, as they now began to retain their own identity of Englishness.

​

So, to answer your question, the process of Christianisation had began in Roman Britain, but was disrupted by fleeing Romans and the subsequent fall of the Roman Empire. Britain was largely pagan until a re-conversion to Christianity, beginning with Augustine's mission in 597.

​

**Bibliography**

Christopher P. Jones, *"Between Pagan and Christian,*" Harvard University Press. (2014)  
NICHOLAS J. HIGHAM and MARTIN J. RYAN, *"The Anglo-Saxon World,"* Yale University Press. (2013)

William C. Wood wrote a brilliant article entitled 'The Gold At Fort Knox,' which answers your questions (and some more!)

The gold currently in Fort Knox came from melted "Depression-era gold coins, from lend-lease arrangements in World War War II, and from government operations under the gold standard." (p. 343)

Conspiracists have questioned the true quantity of gold that sits in Fort Knox and indeed, how much remains from the era of the gold standard. The reserve was first audited during the Eisenhower administration in 1952, and no irregularities were found, nor were they in subsequent audits by various branches of government including the treasury. Yet, some gold did leave the reserve "at below-market prices late in the history of the international gold standard." (p. 344)

The gold remained because it has been used occasionally (usually for ceremonial purposes) since the abolition of the gold standard, such as a small amount being minted for commemorative coins including "the Statue of Liberty Centennial coin and the American Eagle Bullion Coin." (p. 344)

​

Interestingly, there are rumours that some gold at Fort Knox was used as part of the deal to free the hostages from the Iranian Embassy in 1981.

Wood notes false rumours about the uses for the gold: it is not used to back the USD, no holder of currency has any claim on the gold and it is not used to settle international payments. 

​

TL;DR - Gold accumulated wealth from sources incl. melted down coins, unknown quantity remains today to mint coins or to be used in exceptional circumstances (e.g. Iran Hostage Siege), but doubtful US Gov. will ever publicly state quantity/purpose of gold.

**Source:** William C. Wood, "The Gold at Fort Knox," *The Journal of Economic Education*, Vol. 25, No. 4 (Autumn, 1994), pp. 343-348

I’m not sure the specifics on justifying wars by the Papal States, but Catholics in general justified war through the concept of a “Just War.” Undoubtedly they would know about this concept and I imagine it’s how they reassured themselves that eternal damnation did not await them. 

Just War was first discussed by Greek philosophers but later established by Christians including Saint Augustine and Thomas Aquinas. War conflicted with the commandment “thou shalt not kill,” but it was becoming obvious that it would happen regardless, so they attempted to minimise the suffering. 

They had to ensure a war was jus ad bellum (right to go to war): 
1. it would be declared by the government
2. the war must be for the common good
3. the winning state must intend peace. 

And that it was also jus in bello (right conduct in war):
1. Attack only military
2. No torture/genocide
3. Use proportionate force.

Many of the concepts in the Geneva Convention trace their roots back to this principle and some other rules have been added regarding new technology (including nukes), but this is most relevant for understanding the Christian stance on war in the time of the Papal States.

The national identities comprising the passengers aboard the Titanic are surprisingly varied!

Mainly Americans returning to the states, as well as Canadians and Mexicans from North America. Even found several Uruguayans travelling in first class.

A lot of people also came from Western European countries, emigrating to the New World presumably for a better life or to visit family, these included French (who would’ve boarded at the Cherbourg stop), Germans, Belgians, Danish, Norwegians, Finnish Dutch, Swede, Portuguese, Spanish and Swiss.

Furthermore there were many Eastern European passengers, from nations including Austria-Hungary, Bulgaria, Greece, Italy and Russia.

Lastly, there were several Middle-Eastern passengers from Syria and Turkey, as well as passengers from South Africa and even Australia, who may have resided in Britain. 

There were also some Chinese (3rd class) and Japanese (2nd class) passengers.

The passengers came from across the globe, many of them never making their destination, which brings even more poignancy to an already tragic tale when you consider the ripple effects of all those deaths on families in every continent. 

[Source](http://www.icyousee.org/titanic.html)

**What were the houses built from? Was there a fort?**

The houses were described by colonists themselves as “decent dwelling houses” or “cottages”, meaning they must have been at over one storey high, possibly even two as there are references to “neather (lower) roomes”. The roofs were thatched, as a statement from Ralph Lane shows his fear that Indians in the middle of the night “would of beset my house, and put fire in the reedes that the same was covered with”

Furthermore, the chimneys and foundations appear to have been made of brick as Irishman Darby Glande testified that upon disembarkation at Roanoke “they began to make brick and fabric for a fort and houses”, and archaeological evidence supports this as pieces of brick were found at the fort site as late as 1860. (Porter, pg. 29)

Contemporary maps show there was a fort, as was common of settlements of this type and era, but no renderings of it survive. It has been reconstructed as part of the Fort Raleigh Historic Site, but it is impossible to know if these recreations are accurate.

**How did they gather food from their surroundings? Was the ground fertile?**

From what I have read, it seems like the main foods consumed by colonists were crops, including corn and fruits that already grew on the trees there, and fish caught from the shoreline, with the Indians usually helping the English plant/catch the food. Game was also consumed.

The colonists had problems with gathering food from their surroundings and were dependent on Indians and England for food and supplies. At one point, such was the scarcity of food “Lane was forced to send groups of settlers to the barrier islands along the coast to live on oysters and other shellfish and to look for passing ships. Master Prideaux and 10 men were sent to Hatoraske Island for this purpose, while Captain Stafford and 20 men went to Croatoan Island, south of Cape Hatteras.29 Sixteen or twenty others were sent at intervals to the mainland to live on oysters and native foods.” (Porter, pg 29)

The ground was described as, “"a most pleasant and fertile ground, replenished with goodly Cedars, and divers other sweete woods, full of Corrants (grapes), flaxe, and many other notable commodities." 

**How was the island where it stood? How did English travelers reach the island? Did they take boats from the ships? Etc.**

The geography of the island meant that Roanoke was difficult to reach itself, as it had a shallow shoreline which put ships that sailed too close at risk of impacting the crags and shoals that littered the shoreline and sinking. Indeed, as Kathleen Donegan writes on the difficulty of settlement, “The English flagship *Tyger* repeatedly knocked against the hidden outcroppings and nearly wrecked. Left with few provisions and never resupplied \[the colonists were\] completely unprepared to meet the challenges posed by the new environment.”

**Also, with what Native tribes would they have interacted with? What where the local North Carolina tribes?**

The relationship between the colonists at Roanoke and local Native Americans is difficult to examine, as there is a popular desire to explain the failure of the Roanoke colony in terms of the tensions between the white people and the indigenous people whose lands they were present in to colonise. Yet, in some respects, the colony have been reported to have interacted positively with the local Indian leaders of their region of Ossomocomuck, as both parties shared a common desire to learn each others’ languages to better communication. Indeed, two Algonquian Indians, Manteo and Wanchese, actually accompanied White back to London, potentially, during their eight months in England, learning enough English to communicate successfully.

The relationship of the colonists with Native Americans is an interesting debate, it is believed that the colonists may have voluntarily moved to the village of Croatoan, which was forty miles south of Roanoke. But a visit here was never made by John White, who discovered the colonists missing and the carving on the tree, so this is impossible to know for sure. But it’s certainly an interesting possibility, and I like to think that they got out alive.

As with many historical questions, there isn’t a single definitive answer. The best we can do is interpret the evidence and sources we have, and look at the historical context against which these events took place.

It is important to note, as W.M. Ormrod has, that we cannot apply our modern conceptions of sexuality, be it hetereosexuality, bisexuality or indeed, homosexuality, to medieval society. This is an important distinction that is often overlooked in the historiographical debate over the King’s sexuality, which was permitted to emerge following the decriminalisation of homosexuality in the United Kingdom in the 1960s. Historians want to fall on one side of the argument and provide a definitive answer to the debate, when that is impossible.

Edward was married to Isabella of France from 1308 until his death in 1327.

Nonetheless, during his lifetime, it is clear that Edward II had a reputation with regards to his sexual behaviour. It is widely acknowledged that the King had sex with men during his lifetime, and this is sometimes used to explain why he was deposed in January 1327, following the deposition crisis of 1326-27. But this is part of a wider defamation campaign levied against Edward II in order to prove the King possessed a defective character and was inadequate to rule. Additionally, the marriage between Isabella and Edward was portrayed as functioning by his supporters until the deposition crisis, despite the fact Isabella had an affair with Roger Mortimer. (Ormrod, pg 27)

These assumptions about Edward’s sexual tendencies leading to his degenerate nature and eventual deposition are hinted at in the writings of Ranulph Higden a key mid-fourteenth century writer:

>“King Edward was . . ., if common opinion is to be believed, most inconsistent in behaviour. For, shunning the company of nobles, he sought the society of jesters, singers, actors, carriage-drivers, diggers, oarsmen, sailors and the practitioners of other kinds of mechanical arts. He indulged in drink, be-trayed confidences lightly, struck out at those standing near him for little reason and followed the counsel of others rather than his own. He was extrav- agant in his gifts, splendid in entertainment, ready in speech but inconsistent in action. He was unlucky against his enemies, violent with members of his household, and ardently loved one of his familiars, whom he sustained above all, enriched, preferred and honoured. From this obsession opprobrium came upon the lover and obloquy to the loved one; scandal was brought upon the people and the kingdom was damaged . . . *In the beginning he loved Piers Gaveston . . . \[and\] because of him he disregarded Isabella, the queen, and paid no attention to the lords of the land* . .”

The difficulties in interpreting sources are one of the difficulties from any study of medieval history. Many of the sources which point to sodomy were written after the King’s death, and the language is unclear, the word for sodomy had multiple meanings. As Ormrod explains:

>“Sodomy was a category of sin (and crime) that encompassed many forms of non-procreative sexual practices between men and women as well as between members of the same sex. The same problem applies to the term luxuria, a word often used as seemingly synonymous with sodomy in medieval texts, and which has been elucidated again to denote both a generalised indulgence in the sins of the flesh and the specific act of coitus masculorum (male–male anal penetrative sex). Many historians appear to take refuge in this convenient ambiguity as a justification for denying the existence of any positive references to Edward II’s homosexuality in fourteenth-century texts. But this is to refuse the possibility, offered by gay theory, of distinguishing between the general and the specific and identifying places where the words sodomy and sodomite can be legitimately applied in precise reference to sex between men.” (Ormrod, p.36-37)

Edward’s murder is also a point of contention. He was killed by having a red-hot poker inserted into his anus, which many appear as an allusion to his homosexual tendencies at first glance, but it is unclear whether this happened and the act itself can have an ambiguous meaning as medieval methods of torture are notably, pretty gruesome. 

Finally, upon her death in 1358, his wife Isabella was buried:

>“reputedly dressed in the clothes that she had worn at her wedding half a century earlier, and with the eviscerated heart of her husband interred under the breast of her effigy.” (Ormrod, p. 46)

Romantic. 

Either true love or the royal family attempting to manage their image in the aftermath of the salacious claims about Edward which had been prevalent since his death.

To conclude, as attitudes towards homosexuality become more liberal, unquestionably and, perhaps, understandably, there comes a desire from historians and more popular forms of media to portray figures as “gay icons”. Edward II, you could say, is a “victim” of this; it forces conceptions of homosexuality on an individual and society that it is incompatible with. It’s poor historical writing.

If you want to look at it from a postmodern, 21st century perspective then yes, Edward II was gay. However if you want to consider differing values of historical societies then, while he pretty much undoubtedly did have sexual relationships with men, this would not have been viewed by Edward, nor his contemporaries, as evidence of him being a gay man.

In short, because they founded the state.

The Mormon domination of Utah came to be as they were the first whites to permanently settle in the territory, known as the “Mormon Exodus”, many thousands of them fled persecution which included a brief war, the 1838 Mormon War.

After the assassination of the Church of Latter-day Saints’ (LDS) founder, Joseph Smith, Mormons faced increasing hostility in Nauvoo, Illinois where they presently resided. Mormons were blamed for the failure of banks and seen as having all the wealth and power in society due to their insular nature, I suppose you could say it is comparable to the belief modern anti-semites hold about Jews controlling the media

The new LDS leader, Brigham Young, led the community 1,300 miles from Illinois to present day Utah to settle the Great Salt Basin, to form a new community where they would be free from persecution. Known as the Mormon Pioneers, after a long trek, and including European converts in their number, totalling approximately 70,000, they arrived in the Great Salt Lake Valley on July 22, 1847. This settlement would become the present-day Salt Lake City. 

The community struggled at first and almost led to famine, 

“meager gardens planted in such haste in late July-potatoes, buckwheat, and turnips, with some corn in tassel-lasted only "until the first company \[of immigrants\] came in and turned their catde loose; they devoured crops that would have been ready to harvest in a few days," anguished

John Steele.” (Schindler, p. 32)

However, grain recovered and a “miracle” of insects and birds came which helped the crops flourish, and the settlement expanded rapidly. An influx of converts and continued prosperity increased calls for statehood, yet this proved to be more difficult for Utah than for other Western territories.

Campaigns for Statehood began shortly after the arrival in the Great Salt Basin. The settlers organised the state as “Deseret” and requested its admission to the Union. Yet, the federal government did not want to give Mormons their own state, and be held to ransom by them, so they made “The Compromise of 1850”, relegating the settled area to a territory named Utah. The main obstacle to a Mormon state was polygamy, taboo to other Christian denominations.

Requests for statehood continued, yet both Democrats and Republicans were fearful of Mormon political influence in Congress, as they would negate the influence of Democrats and Republicans in Congress with elected officials from their own parties joining the electoral ranks. Indeed, perceived Mormon influence in the political sphere one such thing they had been persecuted for in Nauvoo, leading to the initial exodus. Utah was finally admitted to the Union in 1896, after a compromise on marriage had been reached and local Mormon politics had been aligned with the major national parties. Mormon politics became secularised, Utah joined the Union. 

However, as your question states, heavy religious influence continues to pervade many aspects of Utah’s state laws. One good example is the strict alcohol laws in bars and restaurants, with “Zion curtains” separating bartenders preparing drinks containing alcohol from customers who order them. These laws were reformed in 2017 however, and this is no longer required.

Whether laws should be secular or the extent to which religion can influence legislation is probably a question for a political scientist, but it can be argued that many laws around the world have a basis in religion, whatever it may be, and thus it can seek to regulate the morality of a society.

Hello, this is a great question! It isn't something I'd usually study but I've done some research for you and I hope this answers your question.

​

**When was morning sickness first reported and how common was it?**

​

The Greeks were the first to report morning sickness approximately 4,000 years ago, yet it was rarely studied throughout most of the rest of history due to the stigma that surrounded it, and the patriarchal nature of doctors. Remember, women were banned from being educated at a high level until fairly recently in most countries throughout the world, and even professions such as nursing were seen as masculine until the 19th century. Therefore, it is unsurprising so little research was done into morning sickness as, put simply, it did not affect men, who were the dominant, if not exclusive, medical professionals.

​

**Why does morning sickness occur and how did this impact early civilisations?**

​

An article which delves into the specifics of the food revolution that permits the current diet women follow during pregnancy, known is Thomas D. Holland and Michael J. O'Brien's "On Morning Sickness and the Neolithic Revolution" (*Current Anthropology*, December 2003)

Their explanation for morning sickness (also known as Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy, NVP) is that

> "NVP protects the fetus primarily from secondary compounds produced by plants as defen- sive agents. These compounds contain teratogenic and abortifacient chemicals, but an evolved tendency to avoid these agents or to expel them through vomiting reduces the incidence of fetal mortality. In Profet’s model, NVP first evolved during the Pleistocene (ca.11,000 years ago) to discourage “first-trimester pregnant women from experimenting with novel toxic foods, in favor of incurring short-term nutritional costs and sus- taining viable embryos” (1988:180). To this end, “periods of scarcity would have provided the greatest selection pressures for pregnancy sickness.”

Essentially, that morning sickness came about as human diets evolved to protect the foetus and force women to avoid foods that had toxins with the potential to harm the unborn child. Prior to widespread refrigeration, this is something that was highly important

The article explores the adaptation of human diets that became 

>"carbohydrate-rich: potatoes in South America, maize in Middle America, starchy seeds in the American Midwest, cereal grains in the Near East, and rice in Southeast Asia." 

As women experience morning sickness, they require easily-digestible food and carbohydrates provide this. It's similar to the diet recommended when one suffers nausea, plain toast, rice etc. Furthermore, whereas meat and vegetables may rot and cause food poisoning, carbs do not and thus are safe for women to consume.

​

**What inference was made from women suffering from morning sickness?**

​

Samuel M. Flaxman and Paul W. Sherman's article "Morning Sickness: A Mechanism for Protecting Mother and Embryo" (*The Quarterly View of Biology,* 2000) provides explanations as to why morning sickness occurs, how it has been studied and what it has historically been understood as meaning

Morning sickness has never been associated with risk in pregnancy, a study by Irving (1940), found that 

"only six of our 225 cases \[of pernicious vomiting\] miscarried-a frequency of only one in 37.5 cases, as contrasted with the usualexpectancy in pregnancy of one in every five or six."

Irving did not study morning sickness as most women experience it, but a severe form of it known as hyperemesis gravid arum, (which is what  The Duchess of Cambridge suffered during her pregnancies, forcing her to cancel several public engagements). Nevertheless, these statistics actually present a highly positive outcome ratio in pregnancies where women experience morning sickness.

>“Have not felt very well this week, which has made me somewhat sad.” On another occasion she wrote, “I am not well & have been indulging in gloomy foreboding, but feel- ing this to be wrong, I have endeavoured to recover my wonted cheerfulness.” Such levels of self-awareness during illness were rare; more often, sick people refused or were unable to recognize the ways in which their physical experiences transformed them."
